sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection

items.q: Match the following secondary-cause categories — 1) Celiac disease 2) Hyperprolactinemia 3) Rheumatoid arthritis … A) Gastrointestinal B) Hypogonadal C) Rheumatologic
items.exp: Celiac disease is the GI example, hyperprolactinemia can suppress gonadal function, and rheumatoid arthritis belongs to the rheumatologic group. (Book p896)

items.q: Which is the odd one out in the page's hypogonadal-state group?
items.exp: Acromegaly is grouped under endocrine causes; the other three appear in the hypogonadal-state branch. (Book p896)

items.q: Match the following secondary-cause examples — 1) Ankylosing spondylitis 2) Hemochromatosis 3) Celiac disease … A) Inherited B) Gastrointestinal C) Rheumatologic
items.exp: Ankylosing spondylitis appears with sarcoidosis and rheumatoid arthritis in the rheumatologic branch; hemochromatosis is inherited and celiac disease is gastrointestinal. (Book p896)

items.q: Which is not in the page's endocrine-cause branch for secondary osteoporosis?
items.exp: Cushing disease, hyperparathyroidism, diabetes insipidus, acromegaly and thyrotoxicosis are listed; hypothyroidism is not in that branch. (Book p896)

items.q: Alongside Cushing disease and thyrotoxicosis, the source's endocrine list includes acromegaly and diabetes ___.
items.exp: Diabetes insipidus is the wording printed in this particular list; this should not imply that diabetes mellitus has no skeletal effects. (Book p896)

items.q: Match the following secondary osteoporosis examples — 1) Homocystinuria/Marfan syndrome 2) Turner/Klinefelter syndromes 3) Sarcoidosis/rheumatoid arthritis … A) Inherited B) Rheumatologic C) Hypogonadal
items.exp: The source groups homocystinuria/Marfan with inherited disorders, Turner/Klinefelter with hypogonadal states, and sarcoidosis/rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatologic causes. (Book p896)

items.q: Which diagnosis is the odd one out in the inherited-disease list on this page?
items.exp: Celiac disease is in the GI branch; the other three are explicitly included in the inherited-disease branch. (Book p896)

items.q: The investigation of choice named for osteoporosis is ___; the page additionally mentions trabecular bone score.
items.exp: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry measures bone mineral density; trabecular bone score provides complementary texture-based information. (Book p896)

items.q: A 67-year-old woman without a prior fracture asks about bone-density screening. Which source criterion supports DXA?
opts: Any age only after a hip fracture
Testing only with high serum calcium
items.exp: The source lists women >65 and men >70, in addition to fracture and risk-based indications. (Book p896)

items.q: Assess the DXA indications listed: I Testing is restricted to women >65 and men >70 regardless of risk. II Younger adults with risk factors or prior fragility fractures may warrant testing.
items.exp: The source does not restrict testing to age-based thresholds; symptoms, fracture history and younger high-risk patients also appear. (Book p896)

items.q: Match the following reference comparisons — 1) T-score 2) Z-score 3) Trabecular bone score … A) Age-matched reference B) Young-adult reference C) DXA image texture measure
items.exp: T compares with young adults (25–30 years in the source), Z with an age-matched reference, and TBS reflects image texture rather than a second reference-age comparison. (Book p896)

items.q: Which DXA reference score is generally preferred for a 32-year-old premenopausal woman?
opts: Z-score using an unadjusted elderly reference
items.exp: The comparison definition is useful, but the 'obsolete' label is not a valid universal statement. Z-scores remain important in appropriate age groups. (Book p896)

items.q: A postmenopausal woman has a T-score of −1.8 and no fragility fracture. Which densitometric category fits?
items.exp: A T-score between −1 and −2.5 is the low-bone-mass/osteopenia range; the diagnostic threshold for osteoporosis is ≤−2.5. (Book p896)

items.q: In an appropriate adult, a T-score exactly −2.5 lies in which diagnostic category according to the table?
items.exp: The diagnostic table uses ≤−2.5. A later treatment bullet prints <−2.5, but the boundary should not be lost when interpreting the table. (Book p896)

items.q: A postmenopausal woman has T-score −2.9 and a low-trauma vertebral fracture. Which source category fits?
items.exp: The table pairs an osteoporotic T-score with fracture for severe osteoporosis. (Book p896)

items.q: In the plotted 60-year-old woman, the same BMD corresponds to T-score −2.5 but Z-score −1. Why?
opts: The young-adult reference has higher expected BMD than the age-matched reference
The two scores were measured at different serum calcium values
The Z-score is simply the negative of the T-score
T-score changes only with body weight, not reference population
items.exp: The graph compares one BMD with different reference populations; this explains different standard-deviation distances. (Book p896)

items.q: The biconcave vertebral appearance labeled on the radiograph is the ___ sign.
items.exp: The images show compression fractures and a codfish/fish-mouth vertebra, rather than the hyperparathyroid skull or osteopetrotic patterns. (Book p896)

items.q: A woman has osteopenia but a prior fragility fracture and high estimated fracture risk. Which treatment conclusion follows the source?
opts: Treatment may be indicated despite T-score above −2.5
Treatment is forbidden unless T-score falls below −3.5
A fracture invalidates the DXA result
items.exp: The source includes osteopenia with fracture or raised FRAX risk as treatment indications, not just densitometric osteoporosis. (Book p896)

items.q: Assess FRAX: I It estimates fracture risk using clinical factors, optionally including femoral-neck BMD. II It is a quantity directly measured by the DXA machine, as the source shorthand implies.
items.exp: FRAX is a calculated risk estimate. DXA BMD can contribute, but 'measured by DEXA' is an oversimplification. (Book p896)
